confidence_notes: I ran three web searches: one for the RBA rate and two for current Cuban and Trinidad food and drink prices. The FX value is the RBA's 4.00 pm Sydney AUD/USD rate of 0.6720 for 2026-11-18. A search summary cited this from rba.gov.au, and a third-party RBA mirror (ozfinancehub.com.au) showed the same figure. I did not find an observation for 2026-11-19. Food and drink anchors are based on search summaries, not pages I opened. One summary was of a nomad.watch Trinidad, Cuba page, which listed a beer at about $1.73, coffee at about $2.02 and an inexpensive meal at about $3.61. I treat that meal figure as an understatement for tourists. Several 2026 travel guide summaries put local beer at about $2-3, mojitos at about $3-7 in local bars and paladares, homestay dinners at $8-12 and tourist paladar meals near Plaza Mayor at $15-30 per person. Cuba's prices are volatile because of inflation and its dual-currency and cash economy, and sources range from 2023 to 2026. I found no source for wine, so the wine price is based on its relationship to beer and cocktail prices. Wine is mostly imported and costs more than local beer and rum cocktails. The cappuccino price is uncertain because many venues serve espresso or café cubano rather than true cappuccino. All accommodation anchors come from general knowledge, not searches. Trinidad has few registered hostels, and casas particulares fill much of the budget market, so the dorm and private hostel figures are approximate. Three-star-equivalent rooms are mainly in state-run or joint-venture hotels, whose prices change a lot by season and with the supply situation.
comparable_city_reasoning: I used Trinidad-specific data where I found it and filled gaps with Cuba-wide tourist pricing. Trinidad is a UNESCO-listed tourist town, so I placed it slightly above national averages and in line with Viñales and the tourist parts of Havana for the paladar and casa particular economy. I priced tourist-facing venues, not peso-economy local venues.
